item.title: Tesla's New Roadster Takes Flight After Nearly a Decade of Delays (4 minute read)
item.description: Tesla unveiled its second-generation Roadster sports car on Thursday by having the vehicle launch itself up a curved ramp into a controlled landing. It later leapt over five other Tesla vehicles while twisting in the air. The car is scheduled to enter production in 2028. Tesla has yet to release a price tag. The Roadster can go from a stop to 60 miles an hour in about one second, and it has a top speed of over 230 miles an hour.

item.title: Meta unveils Muse Spark Open, the new top US open weights model — and it runs on two paired Mac desktops (18 minute read)
item.description: Muse Spark Open is an 816-billion-parameter open-weight model that can run on relatively affordable consumer hardware. Meta's benchmark tests used a pair of M5 Ultra Mac Studios with an unknown memory configuration. The model uses a mixture-of-experts design and activates 42 billion parameters for each token. It supports a context of up to 1 million tokens and accepts text, images, video, and audio, but only outputs text.

item.title: Bringing the magic: Google breaks open a bottleneck in quantum computing (3 minute read)
item.description: Google Quantum AI has demonstrated that 'magic state cultivation' works in practice on its Willow processor. Magic states help researchers create the operations they need for going beyond classical computing. Creating high-quality, error-corrected magic states is incredibly resource-heavy. This post details how Google Quantum AI created a magic state cultivation protocol that achieved a 40-fold reduction in errors. The breakthrough is a crucial step towards scaling up quantum computing to practical use.

item.title: How to Train Your Robot (22 minute read)
item.description: Training an AI model fundamentally requires lots and lots of examples of something being done correctly. Creating this data for training robots is expensive, and companies need a lot of data to train competent models. Large language models showed the benefits of scale when training models. Researchers are now working hard to gather enormous amounts of robot task training data in the hopes of seeing the same sort of trends with robotic capabilities.

item.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to reverse engineer hardware (10 minute read)
item.description: Developers are using Claude to debug hardware issues. AIs can read thousands of lines of USB capture, notice sequence repeats with one byte changing, make suggestions on what that byte means, and write the tests to confirm its suggestions. A human is still required to decide what to build and check that the fix runs on real hardware, but AI takes away a lot of the slog. The post includes a link to a harness with a small set of tools that help with reverse engineering Linux drivers.

item.title: New trend of building “internal vibe-coding apps” at tech companies (6 minute read)
item.description: Tech companies are building internal vibe-coding tools for non-engineers. It's not that complicated, it gets higher adoption than vendor products, and it helps build out more AI intra expertise in-house. Building an internal vibe-coding tool is a tiny investment that can result in better, more custom tools than with vendor products, and companies don't have to wait on vendors to build what's needed. It's also a lot safer to expose internal data sources to internal tools.

item.title: How Codex Happened (45 minute read)
item.description: Codex started as a scrappy effort to build an AI software engineer. The team building it had launched a version in the cloud, but it didn't find product-market fit. OpenAI took the project and made it the centerpiece of its comeback. This post tells the inside story of how Codex was created.

item.title: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt (4 minute read)
item.description: CoreWeave has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure buildout. Stock and bond investors are now showing signs of being concerned about AI overspending and debt levels. Yields on CoreWeave debt continue to climb. The spread on its five-year credit default swaps has soared. No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, but the cash flow needs to arrive to justify all of the capex spending.

item.title: The Making of Grand Theft Auto VI (28 minute read)
item.description: GTA VI is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment releases in history when it comes out on November 19. Its immediate predecessor is the best-selling nonmobile game of all time. The game's release is causing other entertainment companies to delay products until next year because they know GTA VI will suck up the planet's attention for most of November. It will almost certainly be the most expensive video game ever created. This article looks at how Rockstar Games built what is expected to be the biggest video game blockbuster of all time.

item.title: Anthropic Says Revenue Jumped 45% to $16.8 Billion in Third Quarter (4 minute read)
item.description: Anthropic told investors recently that the company's revenue for the third quarter jumped about 45% from the prior quarter to $16.8 billion. The AI lab is currently pursuing what may become the largest-ever initial public offering. Its IPO could value the company at $2 trillion. The San Francisco company is expected to begin trading as early as next month. A successful launch from Anthropic could reopen the door for other listings and provide a vote of confidence for the industry.

item.title: 28 Miles and Counting: NASA's Perseverance Rover Sets a Mars Driving Record (7 minute read)
item.description: NASA's Perseverance rover has now driven 28.1 miles on Mars' surface, surpassing the distance that Opportunity covered from 2004 to 2018. Perseverance landed on Mars in February 2021 and has been traveling in and around the Jezero Crater since. It was set to surpass the driving record back in August, but it came across some interesting rocks, so it dawdled for two months. Perseverance most likely still has many miles to go in the coming years. This article contains some of the highlights from its drive so far.

item.title: Things are finally looking up for NASA's first missions to Venus in a generation (13 minute read)
item.description: Two NASA missions are on track to launch to Venus in the early 2030s. The Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging (DAVINCI), which will send a parachute-assisted descent probe through Venus' atmosphere, is now scheduled for launch in December 2030. The Venus Emissivity, Radio science, InSAR, Topography, And Spectroscopy (VERITAS) mission will launch in November 2032 to map the Venusian surface by radar from orbit. The European Space Agency is building an orbiter for launch to Venus in 2032, and Rocket Lab plans to launch a privately funded probe as soon as next year to search for signs of organic material in the planet's clouds.

item.title: Code you didn't write (3 minute read)
item.description: Being able to tell clean code from messy code is still useful, but it's becoming something that tools can help with. Knowing what shape a program should have before anyone writes it is something AI still can't do yet. The best way to get better at AI coding might be to spend more time thinking about problems and less time thinking about prompts. The programmers that get the most out of these tools already knew what they wanted.

item.title: Agentic Verification (18 minute read)
item.description: Giving AI agents a way to independently verify their work heavily improves the quality of output. Write end-to-end tests that simulate real user flows and act as the ground truth. Use property-based testing to specify what should never happen and generate thousands of test cases that attempt to break those constraints. Require tests to run quickly and deterministically so that agents retry when the loop is slow or unreliable.

item.description: SpaceX plans to perform as many as 456 launches and 912 landings at its Texas facility each year. The company's CEO, Elon Musk, has been open about the company's intent to launch Starship as rapidly as possible in the future. He has claimed that, in less than a decade, SpaceX will be able to launch Starship more than once every hour. SpaceX recently announced plans to invest as much as $100 billion to build a massive launch site in southern Louisiana to support rapid Starship launches.

item.title: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient (5 minute read)
item.description: Science Corporation's vision-restoring chip, PRIMA, is commercially available in Europe for patients who have lost their sight to an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration, but the company believes its approach can be applied to multiple diseases. It recently implanted the chip in a patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. The company's work with PRIMA is part of a broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface. It envisions a future where BCIs expand into a wide range of medical technology applications rather than just being used to control computers.

item.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic (23 minute read)
item.description: Anthropic was being bottlenecked by developer infrastructure built for human scale, so it built an in-house version control system called Scion to support its next stage of growth, and fully migrated its monorepo from git in five months. It also built and shipped a code review surface, code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. Anthropic averaged about 2,500 code changes merged per day in May. It now merges over 30,000 per day, and the rate of growth isn't expected to slow down anytime soon.

item.title: How to be more ambitious: A tutorial for humans with models (8 minute read)
item.description: There are four types of ambition. Speed gets the same work done in less time. Altitude involves going up in abstraction and considering the outcome rather than the individual task. Depth considers a task the way a field-leading expert would, going one level deeper and touching the underlying data, tools, and problems. Range draws on multiple fields rather than just the one the task might need at the surface using knowledge, tools, and techniques you normally wouldn't.

item.title: Were we blue-collar workers all along? (3 minute read)
item.description: Blue-collar workers typically do the hands-on labor of making or fixing stuff. Software developers have tried to separate themselves from this category, but they also make or fix stuff, just in bits rather than atoms. Just like electricians or carpenters, software developers must spend years practicing their craft in order to become skilled and sought-after. Just like anyone else in a skilled trade, software engineers can be outpaced by technology.

item.title: Amazon has over 1 million robot workers. What's next for human employees? (23 minute read)
item.description: Amazon already has more than a million robots working in its warehouses, and it is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years. Amazon is also the second largest corporate employer in the world. The company's executives say the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce, but labor advocacy groups and independent researchers say the warehouse automation is not all upside for the humans working alongside robots. It can get complicated when humans are expected to keep pace with their robotic counterparts.

item.title: Is ‘Attention' the Essence of Intelligence? (14 minute read)
item.description: Research suggests that human thought is not purely linguistic. More brain regions light up than just the areas associated with language when we are thinking. Language may be how we communicate about the world, but our thoughts seem to draw on many other areas outside of the brain's language networks. AI's ability to translate effectively means that it can understand, in some sense.

item.title: Why WebMCP matters (12 minute read)
item.description: Co-browsing needs to work really well for users for the web to succeed in the agentic age. WebMCP enables sites to provide agents with direct JavaScript tools they can call to accomplish tasks, which makes direct interaction significantly faster, better, and cheaper. item.title: China's Delivery Robots Are Learning to Tackle the Night Shift (11 minute read)
item.description: Shenzhen opened access for nighttime deliveries by driverless vehicles in March. Night operations make otherwise idle vehicles and infrastructure productive. It also means quieter roads, reduced pedestrian traffic, and lower congestion. Driverless vehicles eliminate the cost of a human: they don't need night shift wages, they don't get tired, and they don't need to be paid extra for driving in the rain.

item.title: Problems in 22 scientific fields had solutions hiding in plain sight. An AI has found them (7 minute read)
item.description: Borrowing an idea from one research discipline to solve a problem in another is an age-old scientific trick. However, such clever leaps are rare because researchers don't tend to spend their time researching fields outside of their expertise. AI can easily hop between fields. BootLoops is a harness that can spot and solve problems in seemingly unrelated fields that share the same mathematical structures at massive scale. Researchers recently released 36 preprints produced with BootLoops covering a wide range of topics, including figuring out the age of sunspots, analyzing government health policies, and attempting to decipher a mysterious medieval manuscript.

item.description: Apple plans to introduce a touch-screen MacBook and a new iPad mini on or around October 27. item.title: SpaceX Makes Big Play to Become a Wireless Carrier (3 minute read)
item.description: SpaceX will pay investment firm Grain Management about $8 billion in cash for US cellular spectrum licenses. The licenses will be for the 800-megahertz band, which is tailored for wireless service from cellphone towers rather than satellites. SpaceX says the new spectrum will help cover places satellite links can't reach. SpaceX still needs some terrestrial infrastructure to use the spectrum for mobile coverage.

item.title: The Start-Up That Wants to Build ‘Microrobots' With AI (8 minute read)
item.description: Atomic Machines is building AI technology that can discover new ways of designing extremely small devices. It is building an automated manufacturing system that turns computer code into a physical device. The company aims to revamp the field of microelectromechanical systems (MEMS), tiny devices made of both electrical and mechanical components. These devices are traditionally manufactured like computer chips, but this limits the possibilities of the technology to the physical properties of a semiconductor.

item.title: Amazon builds 1,000th satellite, will launch space internet service by end of year (19 minute read)
item.description: Amazon's Leo project is nearing several critical milestones. The company recently manufactured its 1,000th satellite and has reached the point where it can build a handful of satellites every day. The Vulcan's upcoming return-to-flight mission will carry Amazon Leo satellites, and another Vulcan rocket is currently being prepared to launch this year with more Amazon satellites. The company is just weeks away from offering a commercial space broadband service for the first time.

item.title: Abstract Warfare: How TSMC Made Its Own Market (17 minute read)
item.description: The most important tech companies are much larger than their original markets. They not only expand their market, but make their own markets as well. These companies achieve this by attacking the abstractions their industry is built on. They change what it takes to participate in the industry and create shared infrastructure out of their competitors' businesses. This allows an ecosystem of new companies to form that both win in the market and are dependent on them.

item.description: OpenAI recently released 372 breakthrough results in the field of mathematics. However, it appears no human has understood any of the proofs yet. Experts reading the proofs say the papers are so horribly written they're impossible to read without AI help. The citations are also often irrelevant and confusing.

item.title: Zuckerberg's Biohub Partners With DOE, NIH to Invest $1.8 Billion in Biological Data for AI Models (1 minute read)
item.description: Biohub, a nonprofit co-founded by Mark Zuckerberg, is working with the Department of Energy, the National Institutes of Health, and other funding partners to invest $1.8 billion in building biological data ready for AI models. The investment is aimed at providing data sets that allow researchers to use AI models to find new ways of preventing and treating diseases. The DOE will invest more than $500 million across five years in lab measurement, modeling, and computation to build an AI-ready open data resource; the NIH will coordinate the contribution of relevant datasets, repositories, and knowledge bases; and Biohub will work with the NIH to standardize the datasets for AI model training.

item.title: In Vienna and Beijing, the First Nuclear Clocks Begin to Tick (6 minute read)
item.description: Two independent teams in Vienna and Beijing have simultaneously built the first clocks that keep time by counting the squishing and unsquishing of the atomic nuclei of thorium. The clocks are so precise that they only lose one second once every few million years or so. Nuclear clocks have the ability to search for certain kinds of dark matter. If a particle of dark matter passes through the thorium nuclei, it could register as a wobble in the nuclear clock's otherwise steady tick-tock.

item.title: Influence without authority (4 minute read)
item.description: Super ICs gain influence by repeatedly doing the unglamorous things. Over time, making the work better, making the story clearer, and making it easier for other people to succeed changes how people behave around you. Authority is a natural side effect of being the person others rely on. Focus on sharpening your craft, turning ideas into stories people can retell, packaging your thinking so it travels without you, and helping your peers hit their goals.

item.title: Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging (12 minute read)
item.description: Readers need a compelling reason quickly to continue reading. The reader should be able to read an article from start to finish without clicking links or hovering for tooltips. Avoid presenting articles as a follow-up to a previous article. Drop the formality and write the way you speak in real life. Test articles in mobile view, and use browser testing tools to find low-contrast text to improve visibility.
